title: Extension points and maintainable code
idea: Extensible code takes new behaviour as new classes at a seam (an interface where new code plugs in); maintainable code keeps changes small, local and testable.
points: Find the axis of change first; put the seam only there.
An interface plus an injected list lets new rules arrive without editing old code.
Boolean flag parameters signal a missing seam; callers can swap them silently.
Small named classes make reviews, tests and traces point at one place.

steps.caption: The composition root decides which rules exist and in what order. Nothing else does.
`Pricer` reads the `Cart` and knows rules only through the `PriceRule` interface.
Each rule is one small class with one job. Each is testable alone.
A new rule is a new class plus one line in the root. `Pricer` is never edited.
Maintainability bonus: `Pricer` traces each rule by name, so a wrong total points to one class.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: Rules hidden behind boolean flags. A swapped argument charges the customer more, and nothing complains.

walk.text: Three booleans in a row. Every new rule widens this signature and every call site.
All rules live in one method. Editing one risks the others, and ordering is implicit.
The caller meant coupon but passed holiday. Both are `boolean`, so it compiles.
Look at the output: a coupon holder pays more than the list price.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Rules plug into one interface. Named tags remove the flag mix-up, and the trace shows each rule's effect.

walk.text: An `enum` tag cannot be passed in the wrong slot. The record copies the set defensively.
The seam: one small interface for the one thing that keeps changing.
Each rule is a record with one job that rejects nonsense values. Adding one never touches the others.
`Pricer` takes rules by constructor injection and copies the list, so callers cannot mutate it.
The loop logs every step, then clamps the total so stacked discounts never go negative.
Order matters and is visible: discounts run before the surcharge, in one place.

pitfalls: Adding seams everywhere "just in case"; unused seams are indirection nobody can follow.
Methods with several boolean parameters; callers swap them and the compiler cannot help.
Rule order buried in `if` chains; put the order in one visible list.

quiz.q: New discount types ship monthly, tax rules change yearly, and the currency never changes. Where should the extension point go?
options: On discounts, the axis that changes most often
On currency, so a second currency is cheap later
Nowhere; one method with flags is simpler
On every class, so anything can be swapped
quiz.why: Seams cost indirection, so place them where change is frequent and likely. Discounts change monthly; currency has no evidence of change at all.

takeaway: Put one stable seam where change happens; keep each change small and local.
